notes: \cpara{Opens with the reader's objection that April 1st is already April Fools' Day.}
\cpara{Turns the objection into the plan: the day of hoaxes will be ``the ideal cover.''}

\cpara{The diagnosis, from the previous day's post, ``The Beauty of Settled Science'' (24 March 2008), which said that ``Newsworthy'' science ``is often based on the thinnest of evidence and wrong half the time.'' Later evidence supports the point; see the notes on that post.}
\cpara{Draws the consequence for readers of science news: they see neither the solid results nor the understandable ones.}
\cpara{The proposal: journalists report old, neglected science ``under the protective cover of April 1st.''}

\cpara{Three sample headlines: Archimedes on why boats float, Euler's proof (1736) that no walk crosses each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once, and the link between breathing and burning, the subject of the author's ``Universal Fire.''}
\cpara{Says the three headlines describe events that happened, only not yesterday. The bridges and the breathing are real history. For the bathtub, see the note on the next paragraph.}
\cpara{Argues that old breakthroughs can be understood without a degree, because they come early in the chain of discoveries, and gives Archimedes as the case.}

\cfact{The Eureka story concerns a different problem. In the version first written down by Vitruvius, about two centuries after Archimedes, the bath showed Archimedes how to measure the volume of King Hiero's golden crown and so test whether it had been mixed with silver. The relation it illustrates, displaced water equal to submerged volume, ``is not what is known as Archimedes' principle,'' which concerns buoyancy (Wikipedia, ``Eureka (word)''), and some scholars doubt the story. Archimedes did explain floating, in \textsc{On Floating Bodies}; the bath and the ``Eureka!'' belong to the crown.}

\cpara{Gives the reason old science matters: all later science is built on it. The first sentence repeats, nearly word for word, a sentence of ``The Beauty of Settled Science.'' The film comparison is the post's own: news of the frontier alone is like the last quarter of a film seen without the rest.}
\cpara{Introduces the editor's objection that readers will not be interested.}
\cpara{Answers with the link-voting sites: readers vote up explanations of old science. No example or figure is given. The line about selling drugs to make payroll is a joke.}
\cpara{States the larger idea: a good new explanation of old science is itself news. This is the substantive proposal, and it does not need April 1st.}
\cpara{Steps back to the holiday as a first step and waits to see whether journalists take it up. I found no report that any journalist took it up.}
